summary: Updates RFC 9171 to clarify that Bundle Protocol Version 7 agents are expected to use the IANA Bundle Administrative Record Types registry to identify and document administrative record types. It also designates code points for private and experimental use.

eli5.summary: There is a list where each kind of status message gets a number. This says everyone should use that list and sets aside some numbers for tests.

questions: bundle protocol administrative record types registry
bpv7 private and experimental code points
what are bundle protocol administrative records
subtitle: Designates code points and clarifies registry use for Bundle Protocol administrative records.

tldr.problem: RFC 9171 (Bundle Protocol Version 7) identified an IANA registry for administrative record types but did not clearly specify which code points apply to BPv7 or reserve ranges for experimental and private use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9713 updates the registry to include a Bundle Protocol Version column, reserves code points for private and experimental use (64384-64511 and 64512-65535), and clarifies that BPv7 agents must use the registry to identify record types.
tldr.outcome: BPv7 implementations have clear guidance on which administrative record types are available, and experimenters can safely use private code points without risking collisions.

today: RFC 9713 is the current standard for Bundle Protocol administrative record allocation. BPv7 agents must consult the IANA registry when implementing or recognizing administrative record types.

sections.title: Administrative Records in Bundle Protocol
sections.content:
The Bundle Protocol (BP) is designed for delay-tolerant networks where long communication delays are normal—such as deep space networks or disrupted terrestrial networks. BPv7 agents (routers) send administrative records to communicate status information: delivery reports, custodian signals, or health checks.

Each type of administrative record has a code point (a number). RFC 7116 created an IANA registry for these code points, but when BPv7 was published in RFC 9171, it did not clearly map which code points applied to which BP version or reserve ranges for experimental use.
sections.eli5: Routers send status messages labeled with numbers. The list of numbers was unclear about which ones BPv7 could use.

sections.title: Registry and Code Point Allocation
sections.content:
RFC 9713 updates the Bundle Administrative Record Types registry to include a BP Version column. Each entry now shows whether it applies to BPv6, BPv7, or both. The document also reserves three ranges for BPv7:

  • Code point 0: Reserved (like BPv6)
  • Code points 64384-64511: Reserved for Experimental Use
  • Code points 64512-65535: Reserved for Private Use

These reservations follow RFC 8126 conventions, allowing vendors and experimenters to use code points without colliding with allocated values.
sections.eli5: The list now clearly says which codes work with BPv7. Some codes are set aside for tests and for company-specific uses, so people don't bump into each other.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content: BPv7 implementations must consult the IANA Bundle Administrative Record Types registry to determine which types are supported. When a bundle contains an unknown or unsupported administrative record, the agent must ignore it gracefully without failing the bundle delivery. This design prevents one unrecognized record type from breaking the entire protocol.
sections.eli5: If a bundle arrives with a message type you don't understand, just skip it. Don't break the bundle delivery.
